messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi Patel had worked as a paramedic in Chicago for more than three decades, and for most of that time he had thought of himself as the kind of man who could stay steady when others could not. That belief changed on a winter evening when he and his partner were called to a warehouse district site after a spill from a damaged industrial container. The air inside the loading bay had a sharp chemical sting, and the first thing Ravi noticed was the smell of alcohol mixed with something metallic and bitter. Within minutes his throat burned, his eyes watered, and several workers began coughing as the corridor filled with darkness from a power failure that made the narrow space feel even smaller. Ravi had later said that what made the scene unbearable was not only the toxicity itself, but the helplessness of being there in his uniform and still not being able to keep everyone safe. The memory of that night now returned to him with startling force whenever he walked past a hospital entrance, heard an ambulance pull up, or even glanced toward a dark hallway at work; sometimes the memory came on without warning from something as ordinary as a passing whiff of alcohol-based sanitizer. When it arrived, he did not experience it as a distant recollection but as a full return of the same terror, his body jolting as if he were back in the warehouse, and he would have to stop whatever he was doing because the emotion became too overwhelming to manage.

In the months after the incident, Ravi found himself spending a great deal of time replaying every decision he had made that night, trying to work out how it could have been prevented. He would lie awake at home after a shift, turning over small details he believed might have changed the outcome, and the rumination gave him a grim sense of control even as it wore him down. That habit of mental review came to structure his days: if he could keep his mind busy with endless analysis, he would not have to sit alone with the memory and the wave of fear that came with it. He also began keeping himself constantly surrounded by people. At home he sought out his wife, children, neighbors, and even casual company from coworkers, and on days off he made sure not to be alone for long. He had come to believe that isolation left him vulnerable to being ambushed by the memory, and being with others gave him a kind of cover, even if he did not talk about what was happening. Yet the more he tried to manage the experience by filling every hour, the more the memory seemed to break through when he least expected it. A smell in a supermarket aisle, the dimness of the garage at dusk, or a glimpse of medical equipment could suddenly pull the full event back into the room, and each intrusion left him more determined to avoid places that reminded him of that night.

Ravi’s efforts to shut out the reminders gradually narrowed his world. He began avoiding hospitals except when absolutely necessary, took longer routes to stay away from ambulance bays, and started delaying routine physical examinations because the exam room, the white walls, and the sound of medical staff moving in the corridor all felt too close to the scene of the spill. At work this became harder to manage. As a paramedic he could not completely escape the settings that now unsettled him, but he became vigilant about where he stood, how dark a hallway looked, and whether an alcohol smell lingered in a room after cleaning. That constant monitoring kept him on edge, and the very things he scanned for—workplace hazards, dark spaces, the sharp scent of alcohol—were the same cues that brought the memory rushing back. Once the memory surged, it strengthened his need to avoid even more, and he would redouble his efforts to stay busy, stay in company, and keep away from medical environments. In turn, those strategies made the reminders feel more immediate: the less he allowed himself to enter a hospital or sit quietly alone, the more foreign and threatening those places became, and the more power they seemed to have when he could not avoid them.

By the time he came for help, Ravi was exhausted by the strain of living this way. He still functioned, but only by arranging his life around avoidance, constant contact with other people, and repeated mental revisiting of the spill, and he felt increasingly ashamed that his work as a paramedic now carried him into the very settings he feared most. What brought him in was the sense that he could no longer keep tightening the circle around himself without losing more of his life and his marriage. He was most afraid that one unexpected smell, one dark corridor, or one routine examination would open the memory again and leave him flooded with the same terror in front of other people. At the same time, he was hoping that treatment might help him bear the memory without having to outrun it, and that he could return to work without feeling that every hospital doorway was waiting to pull him back into that warehouse.
